speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: While smoking rates have decreased from over 18% in the 1990s, they have stagnated at around 12% to 14% in the last decade.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Singapore adopts a multi-pronged approach to tackle tobacco addiction.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This includes public education, taxes, tobacco control laws, regulations on smoke-free areas and help for smokers to quit.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In recent years, we have enhanced our control measures.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Our goal is to denormalise the use of tobacco products over time.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: First, let me elaborate on the proposed increase in the Minimum Legal Age (MLA) for tobacco from age 18 to 21 for the purchase, use, possession, sale and supply of tobacco products.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 2 of the Bill inserts a new definition of "under-aged person" in section 2 of the Act, to provide for a phased increase in the MLA.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Consequently, provisions in the Act that refer to "persons aged below 18 years old" would be amended to an "under-aged person".

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The details of the changes are in clauses 3, 4, 5 and 9 of the Bill.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We are increasing the MLA for tobacco for several reasons.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: First, adolescent brains are especially vulnerable to nicotine addiction.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This is according to a 2015 report by the US Institute of Medicine.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The 2012 US Surgeon-General's report also showed that the younger someone tries smoking, the higher the probability of him becoming a regular smoker.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Smokers who start earlier also find it harder to quit smoking later in life.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Close to 95% of smokers had their first puff before they turned 21, 45% of smokers became regular smokers between their 18th and 21st birthdays.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Based on HPB's student health surveys, among youths below 18, two-thirds of smokers get their tobacco from friends and schoolmates.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Raising the MLA to 21 will mean that retailers cannot sell tobacco to youths between their 18th and 21st birthdays, thereby denying such youths and those in their social circles easy access to tobacco.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We know that social and peer pressures strongly influence youths to start smoking.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: By raising the MLA, we are further denormalising smoking, particularly for those below 21.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This will further reduce opportunities for youths to be tempted and take up smoking before they reach the age of 21.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We have consulted extensively on the MLA increase.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There is strong support from all segments of society, from youths, parents and businesses.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Nonetheless, during the transitional years from now till 2021, we will encourage all youths to refrain from smoking as smoking is harmful.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Quitting is a journey and it will take time for smokers to successfully quit.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The Health Sciences Authority (HSA) will be distributing the new "no-sale of tobacco to underaged persons" signages and educational materials to all tobacco retailers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We will continue to work together with tobacco retailers, schools, Institutes of Higher Learning and agencies like MINDEF and MHA to ensure smooth implementation of the MLA increase.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: During the public consultation, some have raised concerns that youths will turn to the illicit market for cigarettes if they are unable to buy cigarettes legally.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We will work with Customs and relevant agencies to monitor the situation regarding illicit trade and step up enforcement and educational efforts.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Next, MOH will further tighten control over emerging and imitation tobacco products to protect our young and the general community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: At present, the importation, sale and distribution of shisha and other emerging tobacco products, such as smokeless tobacco, as well as imitation tobacco products, such as e-cigarettes and other types of vaporisers, collectively known as Electronic Nicotine Delivery Systems or ENDS, are prohibited.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The purchase, use and possession of these products are, however, not prohibited currently.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The World Health Organization has urged countries to regulate ENDS, including banning them where feasible.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Twenty-eight countries, including Australia, Brunei and Switzerland, currently ban the sale of ENDS.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To tighten regulation of emerging and imitation tobacco products in Singapore, clauses 6 and 7 of the Bill provide for new subsections under sections 15 and 16 of the Act respectively to prohibit the purchase, use and possession of these products.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: First, ENDS and all tobacco products are harmful to health.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: ENDS produce toxic substances in the vapour, including carcinogens, which increase the risk of cancer of the throat, stomach and bladder.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: ENDS also contain nicotine, which is highly addictive.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: It is well-known that nicotine has harmful effects on fetuses and brain development in adolescents.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There are claims that ENDS are less harmful than cigarettes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Some of these actually come from research sponsored by the tobacco industry.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: So-called lesser-harm tobacco products still expose the user to toxic substances that are harmful to health and keep the user addicted to nicotine.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Second, we do not want ENDS or other emerging tobacco products to become entrenched in Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We have seen an exponential increase in the number of people using ENDS in other countries.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The use of e-cigarettes among students has also increased significantly in countries, such as New Zealand and the United States.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Overseas, tobacco companies are increasingly marketing ENDS the same way as tobacco products were marketed.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There is also growing evidence that ENDS manufacturers are targeting the youth market, for example, by using flavours, such as chocolate, strawberry and mint, and with sleek videos and marketing them as trendy choices.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Third, ENDS can be a gateway or "starter product" which gets the user hooked on nicotine and lead to cigarette use later.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Another study showed that among more than 19,000 Canadians, aged 14 to 18 years old, those who used ENDS were twice as likely to go on to regular smoking.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Other studies in England, Scotland and Poland similarly support this "gateway effect".

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: MOH has received feedback arguing that we should consider allowing the use of ENDS by smokers to quit smoking.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We have already approved nicotine replacement therapies, such as nicotine inhalers, gum and patches, to help smokers quit.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These are registered as therapeutic products under the Health Products Act.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Such products have undergone stringent evaluation of their safety, quality and efficacy as a smoking cessation therapy prior to registration.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: While there are some studies which suggest that e-cigarettes may help smokers to quit, the current limited evidence is neither robust nor conclusive.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: If registered under the Health Products Act, the product will be exempted from the ban in the Tobacco Act.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For smokers who wish to quit, there are proven methods and products, and ENDS have not been proven to be one of them.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Next, I will turn to other amendments in the Bill.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 8 of the Bill provides for a technical amendment to section 18 of the Act, to specifically restrict every licensed retail outlet to having only one point of sale.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This amendment eliminates the need for HSA to specify the location of the point of sale in each licence issued.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 2 of the Bill inserts new definitions of "tobacco product" and "tobacco substitute" to improve clarity.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 6 repeals section 15(6) of the Act, to align the definition of smoking for section 15 with the general definition of "smoking" in section 2(1).

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 10 of the Bill amends section 35 to state that composition sums collected shall be paid into the Consolidation Fund, instead of being retained by HSA.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 11 of the Bill inserts a new definition of section 35A, which provides that persons involved in the administration, collection and enforcement of payment of any composition sum collected under section 34 shall be treated as public officers for the purposes of the Financial Procedure Act.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The changes proposed in this Bill will go towards protecting our population and, especially the young, from the harms of tobacco products.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There is mounting pressure, especially from self-interested parties, to relax our position on ENDS.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin) (for the Minister for Health)
text: I seek the Members' support for this Bill.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am particularly worried that smoking prevalence remains sticky amongst the young.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As Parliamentary Secretary Mr Amrin Amin has just noted earlier in his speech, 95% of Singapore's smokers first smoked before the age of 21 and 45%, became regular smokers between the ages of 18 and 20.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If we were to look at the age of inception, that means, at the age at which smokers took their first puff, the statistics also bear grim reading.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In 2001, our youth smokers started when they were 17.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That was the age when they took their first cigarette.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In 2013, we found out that they were actually taking their first puff at 16 years of age.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And all these occurred despite current legislation which makes it illegal to smoke under the age of 18.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As noted, adolescent brains are more sensitive to the rewarding effects of nicotine.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, young persons who start smoking early are more likely to continue smoking into adulthood and become addicted.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The intensity and persistence of smoking also correlate with how early smoking started.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should take note of the 2008 World Health Organization report which states that people who do not start smoking before the age of 21 "are unlikely to ever begin".

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Bearing this in mind, this leads to the first of my four clarifications.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a result, smokers aged between 18 and 21 at the time the Act is amended will be exempted.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The rationale is to give youth smokers who may be already addicted some time to adjust.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I am of the opinion that such stepped implementation is unnecessary and perhaps too gradual.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If someone who has just turned 18 has also just started smoking, this gradual implementation will continue to allow him/her to buy and use cigarettes until he/she is well and truly hooked.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If we stop this smoker at the early stage of the addiction, it may be easier for him to quit.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, I would like to urge the Ministry to increase the MLA for smoking to 21 as soon as possible.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should supplement our efforts with a stronger public campaign to highlight all the negative impact on smokers' health − from the more obvious damage to the lungs to less widely known disease-causing DNA damage which can last more than 30 years after a person has stopped smoking.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to engage our youths through every platform available as their future can be greatly affected by this life-changing addiction.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, the adverse impact of smoking on our National Service personnel, and the financial and resource burden upon our national health system should also not be under-estimated.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, we also have to consider the impact on tobacco retailers' employees, some of whom are aged between 18 and 20.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With this increase in the MLA, staff aged below 21 will not be able to sell tobacco.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think this is a move in the right direction, as constant exposure to tobacco products in the course of their work could tempt these young persons to try smoking themselves.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Nonetheless, I would like to ask if measures can be taken to diminish the economic impact on these young employees over this period of implementation.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, while I laud the ban on Electronic Nicotine Delivery Systems (ENDS), I am concerned that there are many online vendors.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And I would like to check with the Ministry what its strategy is to control this source of ENDS.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And for my final point of clarification, the Bill proposes to align the penalties for the possession of tobacco products and imitation tobacco products for the purposes of sale to that for import, distribution, sale or offer for sale.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, we should consider imposing fines on the logistics companies used by the importers to motivate them to inspect their cargo more carefully.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: An additional layer of checks would be useful.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, I would urge the Government to make restrictions on tobacco marketing even more stringent by studying the case of Australia and emulating what Australia has done in imposing plain packaging if legally permissible.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This idea has been implemented in Australia, New Zealand, France, the United Kingdom, Norway, Ireland and Hungary.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is promising evidence that plain packaging can change people's attitudes towards smoking and may help reduce the prevalence of smoking and increase attempts to quit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Government will explore this in the next round of amendments.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Once this Bill is passed, we will be in a curious position.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will be illegal to possess e-cigarettes but it would not be illegal to possess and smoke regular cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am certainly not suggesting a ban on normal cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That would, I suspect, lead to consequences like what was seen in the USA in the 1920s when they attempted the prohibition of alcohol.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While there is some division of medical opinion about the extent to which e-cigarettes are less harmful than regular cigarettes, surely, there is no evidence and no one would argue, and surely, it is not the Government's argument that e-cigarettes are as harmful or more harmful than regular cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, after this Bill is passed, it would seem that the possession of e-cigarettes will be an offence, but possession of normal, duty-paid cigarettes will not be.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Earlier this year, I asked a Parliamentary Question (PQ) about the Government's stance on e-cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reply was that the Government will not relax its stance because there is insufficient evidence that e-cigarettes are significantly less harmful than conventional cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reply also stated that e-cigarettes contain similar levels of nicotine as normal cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In my supplementary question, I alluded to a study by the British Royal College of Physicians (RCP) that concluded that there is evidence to suggest that e-cigarettes can reduce harm by enabling smokers to move from a more harmful to a not harmless but less harmful class of products.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Government has any such evidence, it would be useful to share that evidence with the wider public, but to the best of my knowledge, no such evidence exists.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In response to my supplementary question, Senior Minister of State Amy Khor said – and I will quote this in full for a more well-informed debate: "Our concern really is with the fact that allowing the use of such products could attract a much larger group of users, especially among the youths, and that could be the gateway to nicotine addiction and, eventually, smoking.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We note the UK reports but despite reports from the UK, the experience of the US is quite different.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The US Surgeon-General also reported that the use of e-cigarettes is closely associated with cigarette smoking among youths and young adults." There are two distinct points here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first is that legalising e-cigarettes may induce non-smokers to take up smoking of e-cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second is that legalising e-cigarettes may provide a gateway to smoking regular cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I agree with preventing non-smokers from having access to e-cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not want to expand the pool of smokers of any kind of cigarette.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We want to move in the opposite direction.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If e-cigarettes are truly less harmful, allowing non-smokers access to e-cigarettes will enable them to reduce the harm they cause to themselves and others.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The number of people this could benefit is not small − in fact, it is massive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If some of the claims being made about e-cigarettes are even remotely true, for example, the headline claim is that they are 95% safer − this could end up extending the lives of smokers and reducing their suffering.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This could also reduce state spending on treating the medical conditions associated with smoking normal cigarettes, state spending in the form of hospital subsidies and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not easy for smokers to quit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Surely, the humane thing to do is to allow the smokers − both those seeking to quit and reduce consumption − an avenue to use a less harmful product.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I agree with MOH's statement, however, that there is no harmless level of smoking.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What I disagree with is what is the best, most humane path to take on the road towards that goal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, let me come to the clinical evidence about e-cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I quote from their press release: "…the possibility of some harm from long-term e-cigarette use cannot be dismissed due to inhalation of the ingredients other than nicotine, but is likely to be very small, and substantially smaller than that arising from tobacco smoking.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With appropriate product standards to minimise exposure to the other ingredients, it should be possible to reduce risks of physical health still further.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But is the evidence for any policy ever 100% fool-proof?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The point is: where is the evidence that e-cigarettes are as harmful or more harmful than normal cigarettes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reason is well-known among professionals in the field but not among the wider public so much.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The vast bulk of the harm caused by cigarettes is from tar and other harmful chemicals, not nicotine.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nicotine, in and of itself, is not of benign chemical but would seem to be no more harmful in a significant way than many other substances that are perfectly legal, such as alcohol and trans-fats, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To quote from the RCP report: "…among smokers, e-cigarette use is likely to lead to quit attempts that would not otherwise have happened, and in a proportion of these to successful cessation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this way, e-cigarettes can act as a gateway from smoking." There are a number of possible objections to this suggestion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first objection is that there is no evidence that e-cigarettes help people to quit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The RCP study and the Cochrane study I cited state, and I will quote again from the RCP study: "Among smokers, e-cigarette use is likely to lead to quit attempts that would not otherwise have happened…" Public Health England also released a report in August 2015 and I will quote from some of the academics who collaborated on this report.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But this moral hazard argument applies to many other areas of policies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, employers can and frequently do over-declare the salaries of workers on employment passes and special passes and take kick-backs in cash from those workers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we do enforce it by advertising penalties, investigating complaints, prosecuting offenders, encouraging whistle-blowing and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The possibility of moral hazard is not a reason not to enact a certain policy in and of itself.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would only be so if there are no reasonable methods to bring some degree of reasonable control over the moral hazards, downside risk, and if the downside risk outweighs the upside benefit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this case, smokers who enrol into a programme to get access to e-cigarettes could be asked to sign a declaration that they are smokers, have friends or family members sign a declaration, too, and they could be given a detailed questionnaire and, perhaps, even physical tests, if possible, to ensure that they are, indeed, smokers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third objection would be that people could use this technique and procure e-cigarettes through such a programme and sell them into the black market for profit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, each individual, under this suggestion, would only get enough for their own consumption, a controlled amount that could be reduced over time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The supply could be decreased over time to encourage them to quit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would be risky, difficult and costly for a prospective black marketer or syndicate to use this method to obtain such small quantities of e-cigarettes when they can simply resort to the kind of smuggling to bring in quantities in bulk that is often seen in cases where non-duty paid cigarettes are seized by customs authorities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fourth objection would be that e-cigarettes are a gateway to smoking.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My suggestion is not to legalise e-cigarettes for the general public − I cannot emphasise this point enough − but only for confirmed smokers who are trying to quit or reduce smoking.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, this objection is not applicable as it would give access to e-cigarettes only to those already smoking conventional cigarettes, people who have already gone through the gateway, as it were.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But in any case, in passing, I would note the point that the UK RCP study made, which is that they did not find any evidence that e-cigarettes were a gateway to smoking conventional cigarettes or that they normalise smoking.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we can extend the lives of smokers and those exposed to second-hand smoke, if we can reduce their suffering and, at the same time, reduce medical costs borne by the state and individuals, we should explore every option to do so.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have a duty to explore every option to do so.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What standard of evidence would satisfy MOH on this issue if that is the case?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: From championing for designated smoking points to rallying ambassadors to educate and spread awareness, it is my wish for residents to enjoy living in a clean and green environment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: More importantly, good health is crucial for one to lead an active and fruitful lifestyle.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I fully support the view that smoking and the presence of second-hand smoke are detrimental to one's well-being.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is also an immense burden on public health.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am pleased to note that in recent years, the Government has been actively introducing new measures aimed at gradually making smoking a thing of the past.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe this will, to some extent, serve as an additional impediment to discourage teenagers and adolescents, at their most impressionable age, to pick up smoking.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are ample studies, including by the World Health Organization, to indicate that a huge percentage of smokers pick up the habit or get addicted before they turn 21.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Cities across the US are raising the legal tobacco purchase age from 18 to 21.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Experts have rationalised that this would reduce peer pressure to smoke.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, we are catching up with what a number of countries had done.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I should add that this is only a small part of the solution.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Determined young smokers will find ways to get around the law.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They can ask their older friends or even strangers to help them to buy cigarettes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In spite of a smoking ban in many public places, that is not stopping smokers from lighting up, as long as no NEA officer is around to enforce the smoking ban.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Understandably, NEA has limited resources and is unable to station officers throughout Singapore at the right time, at the right place.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the agency would have to think of ways to overcome this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps more education, more campaigns by MOH and more enforcement by NEA.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One way is to make it easier for the public to report illegal smoking.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There should be a dedicated hotline for the public to call in.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Or, better still, use mobile applications like OneService and incorporate a new function that allows people to quickly submit reports on the spot.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Once multiple feedback is received about particular hot spot areas, then NEA can deploy more enforcement officers to book the culprits.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have also had feedback from residents who would dutifully call NEA to report smoking on prohibited premises, such as HDB void decks.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But they told me they did not receive any follow-up on their feedback.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, later on, they would see the culprit committing the offence again.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They told me their feedback was not taken seriously.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Also important is equipping young Singaporeans with knowledge to make informed decisions for themselves.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Our schools are doing a fairly good job imparting the relevant knowledge on hazards of smoking.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There have been several anti-smoking campaigns as well.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, more must be done to highlight the financial and health burden of smoking on the individual, family, environment and the nation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should home in on how smoking negatively impacts the eco-system, from littering to producing of carcinogenic smoke that can assassinate our young children.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, give assistance to addicted smokers, especially those under the age of 21.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In pursuing a smoke-free nation, we must not alienate the smokers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many might have picked up the habit due to external influence and pressure or because they did not know what they were getting themselves into and now find it difficult to quit.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, there should also be more resources to educate family and friends on how they can help their loved ones.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Smokers will require compelling reasons and supportive, accessible platforms to kick their addiction willingly.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A well-informed and conscious decision to quit is more effective than any law and policy to keep the cigarettes away.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I believe that no amount of law can keep both smokers and non-smokers happy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Just two days ago, I had a block party.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A young mother came to share with me her problem.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She lives on the ground floor and, beside her block, there is a staircase that leads to the main road.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And every morning, she says that there are lots of people standing at the staircase there, either waiting for friends or waiting for transport.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And while waiting, they are smoking, puffing away.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And she says that the smoke affects her child very badly because her child has asthma.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She tried to talk to the smokers but the smokers stared blankly at her and looked into the sky and told her that, "This is open air.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: You go and call NEA, lah." I have received another feedback from a resident.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She says that she lives with her father-in-law.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Her father-in-law always smokes in the living room.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She wanted to protect her children, brought her children upstairs, because they live in an executive apartment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But then she says that the smoke went up and she is asking for help.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But her father-in-law smokes in his own home − not against any law.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, I would like to take this opportunity to urge all smokers − be responsible smokers, be more considerate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Before you light up the next cigarette, look around whether there are any other young children, whether the smoke will affect other people, because, in both cases, I can feel that the mothers are so helpless.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For example, there are many places that ban smoking in Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, when there are no NEA officers around, smokers will still light up.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should also step up anti-smoking efforts at IHLs, including educating students on the harmful effects to themselves and to the country.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope smokers can be more considerate towards others.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Before they light up the next cigarette, they should look around to see whether his second-hand smoke will affect his family, friends and neighbours, and be a responsible smoker.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah's quote about our young smokers requires some time for reflection.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.09 pm until 3.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, I would like to bring up the issue of second-hand cigarette smoke, especially those suffered by HDB residents who stay above chain smokers.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Typically, the resident who is smoking will stand near the window and the smoke then blows up to the unit above.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Prolonged exposure to second-hand cigarette smoke can be very harmful.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During the Second Reading of the Community Disputes Resolution Bill in March 2015, Members, such as Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Zainal Sapari, had brought up this issue of second-hand smoke in HDB homes.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And usually, the solution is for the residents to go for mediation.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One of the main shortcomings of mediation is that it will not happen if one of the parties is uncooperative.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While we respect the rights of residents to smoke in their own homes, the right to clean air for the neighbours must also be respected.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, I understand it is unlawful for anyone to exhibit indecent exposure even within their own homes if their neighbours complain.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To the extent where there is evidence to prove that second-hand smoke in the upstairs' neighbours' homes have reached unhealthy levels, then the affected residents can apply to Court for the residents downstairs to take measures to reduce the level of second-hand smoke.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I understand the logic for this decision, which is to provide time for smokers to adjust, I feel that it is even more important and more urgent to prevent any youth from getting started on smoking in the first place.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The risk of addiction by those under 21 necessitates fast and firm implementation to reduce any exposure.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Furthermore, increasing the MLA year by year over the next three years will cause confusion.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I am concerned by the wide availability of cigarettes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One can purchase them anywhere: 24-hour stores, supermarkets, mom-and-pop shops.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is really so easy to lay one's hands on a packet.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Given the tremendous harm smoking and second- and third-hand smoke do to our people, I think it is completely justifiable to reduce the number of stores which are licensed to sell cigarettes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third-hand smoke refers to the residual nicotine and chemicals which accumulate on surfaces and resist normal cleaning.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is what clings to the hair, your clothes and any surface in the vicinity long after the smoking activity itself has stopped.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Research has found that third-hand smoke poses a potential health hazard to anyone exposed to them, especially our young children.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the proliferation of social media, the general public has become more image conscious, especially the youths.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As smoking is so damaging to health, smokers generally end up looking much older than their years.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, by the time a smoker reaches the age of 40, he or she would probably look 10 years older.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can use this awful impact on smokers' visages to encourage smokers to quit.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, I urge the Ministry to work more closely with our Primary and Secondary schools to educate our young on the harmful effects of smoking.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More can certainly be done to inform our children about the evils of cigarettes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry share with us what are the current measures and educational campaigns in our schools and how effective they have been?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, we should look into ways we can educate older family members and friends of our young about not sharing their cigarettes with impressionable teenagers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope the Ministry would consider placing a heavier onus on logistics companies to prevent their services from being used to deliver these noxious products.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is in view of the fact that most of our e-cigarettes have been delivered via Internet orders.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have seen first-hand how the bane of cigarettes has led to many health problems.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In fact, according to the US Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, the number of deaths, directly or indirectly related to cigarette smoking causes one out of every five deaths in the US every year.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That is more than 480,000 deaths in the US alone.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This, compared to drug deaths, which only record a total of 64,000.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: State Express 555 was her brand of choice.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She was an opera singer by training and led an otherwise healthy life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the puffs she took was to lead to a major heart attack and her untimely passing before she could undergo surgery.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He smoked packs, not a pack, but packs daily.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just before my grandmother passed away, he was trying to give up smoking.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But perhaps the grief of losing his mother started him on cigarettes again.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I remember hiding his cigarettes in the garden, doing everything we could to convince him to give up smoking.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He tried, but, like most smokers will tell you, it is hard to break the habit once it has started.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Then, one day, while he was working in Shanghai, he broke out in cold sweat and had chest pains.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A few weeks later, he travelled to Macau.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I was still in the army at that time.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I remember receiving a call from my mother saying something had happened to him.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He had said that it was appendicitis so we flew him home and he almost wanted to down some Po Chi Pills and just head home to rest.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By sheer willpower, we managed to get him to hospital.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the pre-surgery checks, the doctors noticed that there was something wrong with their ECG results.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They changed to another machine and got the exact same results.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What happened next was 24 hours of being in surgery for his appendicitis and, more importantly, for a major heart bypass.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are thankful that the doctors saved him.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He is leading a healthy life with his grandchildren right now.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But others do not have the same benefit like he had.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have also seen friends suffering from lung cancer, a slow lingering death, suffocating, painful, tragic.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These are just some examples, and there are many, of how something sometimes seen as cool or hip to have a cigarette in your hand, can lead to personal health risks and a major burden on our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is also a risk not borne just by the smoker himself, but also by those around them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have one of the strictest regimes in tobacco control in the world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We ban tobacco advertisements, we limit tar and nicotine, we ban shishas, we were the first in Asia to introduce graphic warning labels and we also have a strict Point of Sale Display (POSD) ban.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, while numbers have fallen, as pointed out by the Parliamentary Secretary, we are still amongst the highest in smoking rates amongst OECD countries.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I, therefore, welcome the efforts of the TCASA to further tighten regulations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Should we not have immediate implementation as the best way forward?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we believe that smoking is inherently unhealthy, should we not introduce the MLA with immediate effect?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In fact, as I have mentioned earlier, if we believe that a burden on public health is a major one caused by smoking, should we not ban tobacco completely?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With regard to the use of ENDS, I applaud the Bill's response to these emerging products.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, I would like to ask how exactly will the Ministry police the import and use of these products, especially when travel is now very much a part of the Singaporean lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many travel abroad and purchase items, such as vaporisers and nicotine substitutes, many of which are unregulated overseas and may contain harmful additives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just a few weeks ago, I was at Mount Alvernia Hospital and I saw a vape being used openly.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When the user spotted me looking at him, he stuffed his vaporiser into his bag – something where you cannot really do with a lit cigarette – and boarded the shuttle bus.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He is just one of those I have seen using vapes and e-cigarettes around Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While we do not want to be inspecting every single online shopping parcel entering Singapore or to check every bag of a returning Singaporean at our ports or airports, how will we prevent such items from entering Singapore and being used?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The hon Member Leon Perera quoted a study in the UK on the low risk of vaporisers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The National Institute for Health in the US studied this particular report and came to the conclusion that only 181 self-selected respondents participated in this particular study and many other factors were not included in coming up with the results.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Maybe not now, but perhaps at some point in the near future, such as the regulations that had been put in place by Bhutan since 2004.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I support any efforts to safeguard the health of Singaporeans and to discourage smoking.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Many youths today succumb to smoking for social acceptance by friends or peer pressure or falsely believing that it would reduce stress and for other reasons which they feel are justified.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There is much anecdotal evidence, which we often heard, that the young male adults picked up smoking habits while serving National Service.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Youths below 21 tend to be more vulnerable to fall into such undesirable and unhealthy habits as presently; at 18, they are able to purchase cigarettes freely.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, there is apprehension whether by increasing the MLA, will the desired effects and intended outcome of having fewer young people being addicted to nicotine be realised in the local context.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Increasing the MLA will increase the social distance or age gap from social sources who can buy the cigarettes for them legally, but it may not deter teenagers who have been smoking daily.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The main effect of doing so may simply be to drive 18 to 20 year-olds to find other means of obtaining tobacco, legally or illegally.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, purchase of cigarettes from commercial stores by this age-group will see a decrease, but this will mean that they will simply turn to their social sources, that is, soliciting help from someone who is 21 or above or being offered tobacco by relatives, friends or strangers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: One possible way to "effectively" pass a law to eliminate smoking or its onset in youth could be to introduce stiffer or greater penalties or punishments for the "middlemen" or social sources.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There are existing laws in Singapore as deterrent that penalise underage teens who are caught smoking and teenagers or adult peddlers and commercial stores which sell them illegally.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, there is no safeguard from temptation; temptation aroused by social sources or acquaintances that continually provide easy access to tobacco or cigarettes as a form of temptation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Raising the age limit may potentially be a cosmetic deterrent that will not be effective enough if the availability of cigarettes from social settings in social events is not addressed.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Experimental smoking can stem from peer pressure, as a form of coping mechanism, but likely because these underage teens still think it is cool to smoke, and the Government needs to tackle mindset change in the way they view smokers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Many youths look upon celebrities to be their role models and, therefore, it is important for such celebrities to be promoting abstinence from smoking.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: A series of public awareness campaigns and testimonies by famous sports talents and celebrities will be more impactful and a force to be reckoned with.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It would also be worthy to consider helping individuals make their own decision to stay away from the smoking habit so that they feel empowered.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: HPB pro-quitting campaign in 2014 was useful in the sense that it had moved away from the traditional campaign model of focusing on "anti-smoking" publicity as well as displays of debilitating and ill-effects of smoking on the individual and those around them by instead focusing on empowering individuals who had quit smoking.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: One should feel "more cool" not to smoke or quit smoking completely.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, the Government can consider a campaign that is specifically targeted at youths below 21 years old and understand the psychology of preventing them from catching the habit of smoking at an early age.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to that, there could be more effective publicity put up in public spaces and crowded areas with the hotlines or alternative avenues, such as support groups or services, which current smokers can dial or visit if they ever want to consider quitting.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Our home is the first defence for our youths to stay away from cigarettes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Schools and social places where youths congregate should help in the education and sharing of testimony from fellow youths who had quit smoking and the start of an empowering journey of self-realisation for many other youths who have the intention to embrace smoking.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, public education campaigns will have to be met with sufficient funding so that the media components can achieve the necessary outreach to be effective.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, there can be more local research convened to study the ill-effects of smoking on the fertility of both genders and the effects on foetal development in pregnant women in the local context.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Such facts can add to the realisation of not picking up the habit and, if individuals have done so, there is a possibility of such individuals dropping the habit due to better understanding of the perverse outcomes of smoking.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: From the preventive health perspective, it is important that, as a society, as a caring community, we must put in all efforts to stop our young from being preyed upon by the smoking habit which will result in more chronic and critical illnesses, if left unchecked.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To me, this is a very important Bill − one which complements our current laws against drug consumption and abuse.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my speech, I will address two issues.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One, that adolescent smoking leads to a propensity for drug consumption and abuse; and two, that more needs to be done to curb adolescent smoking.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would go one step further to make it illegal for any person below the age of 21 years old to even smoke a cigarette or other tobacco products.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, I strongly support the amendments to section 11 that prohibit underage persons from using, possessing or buying tobacco products.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Here, I must disagree with the hon Member Mr Leon Perera who advocates allowing controlled use of e-cigarettes.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am not convinced that addiction treatment which has used so-called safer substitutes has worked.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us not forget when we introduced subutex as an alternative to opiates back in 2002.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This use of subutex created a whole breed of addicts and a disturbing increase in the emergence of needle culture among these addicts, even more than that during the peak of the heroin addiction.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The subutex used primarily came from licit or lawful sources and not from illicit sources, because it was meant to treat opiate addiction by General Practitioners.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The results were even more startling when the statistical evidence was sub-divided by age groups.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Associations between smoking and illegal drug use were significantly stronger for young people.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, people aged 12 to 15 who smoked cigarettes were 44 times more likely to use crack, compared with only a twofold risk in those 50 or older." This study involved more than 17,000 respondents.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some may say this study is somewhat dated as it was published 17 years ago.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, another more recent research found that "Adolescent regular smokers showed significantly higher odds of using marijuana, cocaine and heroin", according to a longitudinal study spanning more than 35 years and which involved more than 1,200 individuals conducted by Strong, Juon and Ensminger, published in January 2016.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Research and academics aside, we cannot deny that curbing smoking among the young is not just about preventing them from picking up a bad habit.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is to help them to not pick up any form of substance addiction or abuse, as far as we can help it.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Two persons I know have told me it is easy to buy them and that even students below the age of 18 have bought them, especially so when they are this cheap.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Other than affordability, I have another concern regarding such "Roll-Your-Own Tobacco" products.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: When you see some of our students hanging outside our IHLs, since they can no longer smoke within the premises, and they are smoking, you might begin to wonder if it is just tobacco that they are smoking.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: While these numbers are small, it is still one too many.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: The possibility of having such numbers growing is high.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: I would urge the Ministry to review the public sale of such small and affordable packets of loose tobacco leaves.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: If there is a need to sell such packets of loose tobacco leaves to cater to a select group of smokers who prefer rolling up their own tobaccos, there must be some parity to the price of rolled cigarettes sold in packets.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: If a packet of rolled cigarettes cost more than $10, so should these packets of loose tobacco leaves.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: At this point, Mr Speaker, please allow me to say a few words in Malay.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: (In Malay):   Smoking is a habit that we must continue to eradicate, especially amongst our youths.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Apart from causing health problems and wasting money, smoking is also a time-wasting habit.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Just imagine, a stick of cigarette takes about five minutes to finish.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: If a person smokes 10 sticks each day, around one hour per day is burnt away − burning away the cigarette, burning away money, burning the lungs, as well as the health of that person.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Is this habit not wasteful and highly unproductive?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Data on smoking from the National Health Surveillance Survey conducted by MOH in 2013 showed that the number of Malay smokers is more than twice the number of Chinese or Indian smokers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: In addition, the proportion of our Malay youths under 30 years old who smoke is relatively higher, compared to Chinese or Indian youths.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Studies and research have shown that those who start smoking in their teens are more susceptible to drug abuse.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: If we wish to eradicate the problem of drug abuse, we must also stamp out the smoking habit.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: The amendment Bill that is being tabled is timely.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: One example is the These-Abled group started by Ms Nur Aryssa Jumadin, Mr Mohd Haiqel Jamaludin and Mr Muhd Asyraf Mustaffa, who organised the IQRA Project where religious knowledge is taught using the Qur'an in Braille for the visually handicapped.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: He is a well-known percussionist and a recipient of the Singapore Youth Award 2013 as well as the ASEAN Youth Award 2013.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Mr Riduan used to smoke, but he successfully kicked the smoking habit.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Currently, his time is spent on creating music and enhancing his artistic abilities, which have brought him to the regional and global stage.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, I would also like to propose for the Ministry to review current efforts in curbing smoking among the young and in public places.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: The Health Sciences Authority officers and employees may be authorised to take to task those who flout the laws governing the sale of cigarette or tobacco products, while NEA officers and employees may be authorised to take to task those who flout the laws governing littering, including errant smokers who litter their cigarette butts and ashes around.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: However, at the same time, there has to be a more concerted effort to curb both smoking and littering in public places and should involve more public officers to extend this outreach effort and raise public awareness against smoking and littering, similar to how our Pioneer Generation ambassadors reach out to seniors.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: It would also be useful for MOH to appoint members of the public who are trained to advise and or even issue summons as to errant litterbugs and smokers who continue to litter and/or smoke in prohibited places.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: More importantly, the role of these MOH-appointed representatives is to ramp up outreach and public education against smoking, specifically among our youths.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Granting these appointed members of the public with some level of authority will also help alleviate the demand on our current HSA or NEA officers to carry out similar responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: The remuneration framework for these MOH-appointed members of the public can be similar to that for our PGAs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: The public education and awareness efforts have to continue, as do efforts to reach out to our young to redirect their energies and focus on meaningful activities and projects and away from smoking and addiction. "What hurts more than losing someone is knowing you are not fighting to keep them from harm." We need to continue to fight to keep our children safe from the harms of smoking and drugs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I celebrated my quitting anniversary just last month, on 12 October.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have not smoked for more than four years now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I started smoking when I was about 18 years old and it was during my National Service days between 18 and 21 years old that I smoked the most.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When we debated the previous Tobacco (Control of Advertisements and Sale) (Amendment) Bill, I shared with this House that "research by WHO shows that people who don't pick up smoking before the age of 21 are unlikely to ever start smoking".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a positive and huge step forward.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, I would like to seek some clarifications about other aspects of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, whether details of such cigarettes and data can be shared in this House?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I can attest to the fact that quitting smoking is not easy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I can tell you that looking after twins at 3.00 am is difficult but quitting smoking is more difficult.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Quitting smoking is probably one of the most difficult things that I have accomplished in my life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The withdrawal symptoms are severe and the urge, the craving to have a puff, is extreme.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Having gone through it, I know that people who want to quit need more help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do understand the Ministry's position and fear regarding, one, the gateway effect of allowing such alternative reduced-risk tobacco products; and two, that such products contain similar nicotine levels as traditional cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, on the gateway effect fear, there are numerous studies done and publicly available results which show that this fear may be overstated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Mr Yap pointed out, the Minister's evidence in the March 2017 reply supporting the rise in the use of e-cigarettes amongst US youths ignores the other data trend across the same period which shows a significant decline in the use of cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Most recently, a study by Prof Linda Bauld at the University of Stirling published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, showed that this fear of the gateway effect is overstated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, the study involving data gathered from 2015 to 2017 of youths in the UK, shows that e-cigarette experimentation by teenagers is simply not translating into regular use.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, I do question the argument of youths picking up the habit of smoking via e-cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we increase the minimum legal age and if HSA follows up with enforcement efforts, our youths under the age of 21 will still be protected from access to such e-cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, can the Parliamentary Secretary clarify the scientific basis of this fear of the gateway effect in our policy?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And whether Singapore may be missing out on a chance to benefit from a policy which allows controlled use of alternative reduced-risk tobacco products to continue our fight against smoking?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, I understand that Phillip Morris has a research lab facility in Singapore researching and developing such e-cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, access to primary data and resources for a study partner does not appear to be a challenge.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Shouldn't the answer be about tar and carbon monoxide instead?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Or at least one of the many other chemicals in cigarettes that could harm your body?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And if lower levels of other chemicals are detected in heat-not-burn products, then the same level of nicotine would be a good thing because it would be easier for addicts to switch products because they get the same high while causing less harm to themselves and others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We practise 'reduced harm' policies for other vices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If heat-not-burn products and e-cigarettes reduce harm, we should allow them, and then the health authorities should commit to this and research".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Parliamentary Secretary provide clarifications on the above points raised?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do hope we will also devote more resources into helping people to quit smoking and look into every available means to help them in the quitting process.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Speaker, Sir, much work has been done over the years to curb the scourge of smoking and I appreciate the difficulties of this task as mentioned by other Members.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On one hand, we want to discourage Singaporeans from picking up this harmful habit or kick the addiction.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, we also do not want to drive it underground.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, in my recent house visit, I did check with some residents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They have also pointed out that by having it staggered over three years is a good move.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These include, for example, the illustrations of the harmful effects of smoking on cigarette packaging, the increase in the number of non-smoking public areas and the implementation of non-display at points of sale.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, I would suggest that the authorities consider public education through more intensive media advertisements, such as over the radio, television and the Internet.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand from some of my residents that the recent advertisements on our free-to-air channels which promote upcoming programmes are overly repetitive.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps the Government can consider tapping on these pockets of under-utilised television time slots to run various public education advertisements which share different aspects of the harmful impact of smoking and methods for quitting.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How does the Government check on online purchases and curb online sales by overseas vendors or suppliers?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All these foreign sellers are not within our jurisdiction, how can we take these overseas suppliers to task?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do we have any collaborative enforcement agreements with foreign governments?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The problem here is second-hand smoke, as mentioned, which drifts out and pollute the environment and, especially the third-hand smoke, which are the harmful chemicals which accumulate on surfaces in the vicinity of smokers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is it possible to require smokers to close their windows or require buildings to install smoking cubicles or cabins to solve this perennial problem?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, I would like to suggest that we look at having empowered volunteers, especially the youth volunteers, to help carry out public education and enforcement, similar to the community volunteers who tackle litterbugs.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: I will now address Members' queries on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Ms Joan Pereira asked about the effectiveness of our current measures.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: MOH tobacco control measures are based on best practices recommended by the World Health Organization and are designed to work at multiple levels.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Collectively, the measures work together to reduce smoking prevalence in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: As tobacco use is an addiction, we also do not expect to see significant drops in prevalence immediately after new measures are introduced.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Progress has been made but we need to do more.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Dr Chia Shi Lu, Mr Alex Yam and Ms Joan Pereira suggested to raise the MLA to 21 with immediate effect.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: However, we are mindful of the impact on current smokers between the ages of 18 and 21.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Smoking is an addiction and, even as we encourage smokers to stop smoking, they need some time.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Raising the MLA alone will not eliminate youth smoking.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We will continue to send a strong message to young people to stay away from cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Educational efforts and support for youth smokers to quit must complement legislative measures.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: I agree with what Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar has shared.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We must encourage our youths to devote their time, effort, mind and energy to useful and meaningful activities and stay away from tobacco products.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: This is, indeed, the holistic approach which we have adopted.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: HPB's smoking cessation programmes for youths adopt a strengths-based approach to build confidence for behaviour change.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: In response to Er Dr Lee Bee Wah's question, there are Student Health Advisors trained in smoking cessation who are stationed full-time in 50 schools and Institutes of Higher Learning.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: And Er Dr Lee Bee Wah will be happy to know that there are also Student Health Advisors stationed in schools in Yishun.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: We also work closely with MOE to incorporate anti-tobacco messages into the curriculum.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Youths are also taught skills to refuse cigarette offers in social settings.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: In response to Mr Louis Ng, we have looked at Prof Linda Bauld's study in detail.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: It was actually a cross-sectional study that looked at the situation at one point in time.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: This study design is not suitable for studying the gateway effect.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: There have been studies in the US, the UK and Canada, which followed up with more than 40,000 youths over time and found that e-cigarette users had a greater risk of becoming cigarette smokers.
